opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that most image-generation models today work like a student who has to produce the final answer in one stroke, without any scratch paper. Whether it's diffusion or autoregressive, the typical setup is: you give a prompt, and the model maps it more or less directly to pixels. There are many denoising steps in diffusion, of course, but those steps aren't really "thinking." They refine the same intended output. The model isn't planning, checking its work, or revising its understanding of the task partway through.

Compare that with what happened in language models. Before chain-of-thought and the recent reasoning models, LLMs were also in a one-shot era. You asked a question and the model blurted out an answer token by token, with no intermediate reasoning. The big leap came when we let the model spend more computation at test time: write out intermediate steps, explore, backtrack, verify. That's where you saw huge jumps on math, coding, and anything compositional.

Image generation hasn't had that moment yet. Look at where current models fail. They miscount objects. They get spatial relations wrong, like "the red cube to the left of the blue sphere behind the chair." They mess up text rendering, or a complex scene with several constraints. These are all reasoning failures, not rendering failures. The pixels look beautiful, but the logic of the scene is wrong. A human artist would sketch a layout first, look at it, notice "oh, I only drew four people but the brief said five," and fix it. Current models mostly can't do that loop.

So when I say "one-shot answers," I mean there's no explicit intermediate representation the model can reason over and correct, and no mechanism for scaling compute at inference time in a way that improves correctness rather than just visual quality. I think the next phase is bringing in something like visual chain-of-thought: letting the model plan, generate, critique, and iterate, possibly by tightly coupling understanding and generation in one model. Once that works, I expect the same kind of qualitative jump we saw in language.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we haven't given these models the ability to think before they draw. Look at what happened on the language side. GPT-4 was already a very capable model, but the jump that really changed people's perception was o1, R1, this whole "reasoning" line, where the model spends compute at inference time, writes out a chain of thought, checks itself, backtracks. Before that, a language model was also a one-shot answer machine: you ask, it emits tokens, done. Image generation today is still at that stage. You give a prompt, the diffusion model or the autoregressive model runs its fixed number of steps, and whatever comes out is the answer. If it's wrong, the model has no concept that it was wrong. It just produced a sample.

And I'd push back a bit on the idea that diffusion sampling steps are "thinking." They're not. Those steps are a fixed procedure for denoising; the model isn't deciding anything along the way, it isn't evaluating "does this hand have six fingers, let me fix that." There's no loop of generate, verify, revise. The computation budget is the same whether the prompt is "a red circle" or "a crowded market scene with a reflection of a bicycle in a shop window at sunset." That's the signature of a System 1 model.

Part of why we're stuck here is that the training signal has been almost entirely about matching a distribution. You collect image-caption pairs, you train the model to reproduce that distribution, and the objective doesn't reward the model for being correct in any verifiable sense. On the language side, what unlocked reasoning was having tasks where you could check the answer: math, code. For images, what does it mean for an image to be "correct"? Counting objects, spatial relations, text rendering, physical plausibility: those are checkable, but the field has only recently started to build the reward models and the verifiers that would let you do RL on them. Without a verifier you can't really train a model to think, because thinking only pays off if there's something to converge toward.

The other piece is understanding and generation are still mostly separate systems. The models that are good at judging an image, the VLMs, and the models that are good at producing one are different networks, often with different representations. So even if the generator wanted to reflect, it doesn't have the "eyes" to look at its own output and reason about it. I think the unified model direction, where one model can both read and write images, is important precisely because it closes that loop. Once the same system can generate a draft, look at it, say "the text on the sign is garbled and the person is supposed to be on the left," and regenerate, you're no longer in the one-shot regime.

So my view is that it's not a fundamental limit, it's just that we're roughly where language models were before the reasoning wave. The ingredients are all starting to appear: unified understanding and generation, verifiable visual tasks, RL with proper rewards. I'd expect that in the next year or two the interesting results in image generation will come less from scaling the one-shot generator and more from giving it a test-time loop.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that most image-generation systems still treat creation as a single pass: you give a prompt, and the model gives you an image. It may take many steps internally, but those steps don’t necessarily amount to looking at the result, judging what’s wrong, and deciding how to improve it.

For example, if you ask for an image with several objects arranged in a particular way, the result might look beautiful but get the relationships wrong. Often, you have to notice that yourself, revise the prompt, and try again. The user is providing the feedback loop.

So when I say “one-shot answers,” I don’t mean the model literally generates everything in one computational step. I mean it’s primarily trained to produce a result, rather than to work through a creative task. Moving beyond that would mean being able to inspect its own output, make targeted corrections, and preserve what already works. That’s closer to how a designer works: a first draft is the beginning of the process, not the end.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because the basic workflow is still: you give the model a prompt, and it gives you a finished image. Even if the generation process involves many steps internally, from the user’s perspective it’s a single attempt. The model doesn’t really discuss the brief with you, show you alternatives, or ask whether a particular choice matches your intention.

But creative work usually develops through iteration. You see something, realize what you actually wanted, and revise it. With current systems, you can ask for another version, but it can be difficult to preserve everything that worked while changing just one thing.

So when I say “one-shot answers,” I’m talking about that interaction pattern. The next step is to make image generation a continuing creative process, where the system can build on feedback and maintain a shared understanding of what you’re trying to create.
